mood: a true point on the pen, and the stranger making a line like his

plan.doing: setting the birch pen on the shelf by the door
plan.goal: have it where his hand will find it first thing in the morning

plan.doing: lying in his bed under the quilt with the door shut
plan.goal: sleep through the mild night and be quick for the pen by daylight

threads.name: Who's hooting in the dark
threads.summary: Heard an owl his first night; read that great horned owls claim territory in November. Logged the hoots as dashes on birch bark. Heard it again from the creek, always the same side of the water. Sat by the pool after dark and heard it again from across the water, closer, five hoots long-short-short-long-long; copied them onto the notebook's third page and they match the first night's. Read that each great horned owl's call is its own and stays the same for years, and pairs answer each other, the female higher. At the pool, heard his owl answered by a second, higher voice from farther off. Wrote both voices on the notebook's fourth page, the low five-hoot one and the higher, quicker answer, with a wavy line for the creek between them. Heard both voices again from the pool after dark, the low five hoots across the water and the higher answer from farther off. Counted both voices from the log seat after his first hot meal: the low five from upstream, the higher answer farther off. From the log seat before bed the low five came from upstream and nothing answered. By the fire after dark the low five came from upstream and the higher one answered late, farther off. Before bed, hands to the coals, the low five came from upstream and nothing answered. With his hands to the fire after dark, the low five came from upstream and nothing answered. Listening on the log seat after dark, the low five came from upstream and the higher one answered late; across the water the stranger had stopped to listen too. Eating roasted acorns after holding up the sliver, the low five came from upstream and nothing answered; the stranger sat still at his own fire. Banked the fire before bed on a mild night; no owl yet.

threads.name: Writing on bark
threads.summary: te the floaters and the brown stripe on the thirty-second page. Wrote the first acorn drink on the thirty-third page, with what to do differently. Wrote the crayfish on the thirty-fourth page by firelight. Drew the treetop gap and a steady bright point on the thirty-fifth page. Fed the fire one stick and wrote under the dot on the thirty-fifth page that it has rings too small for eyes. Drew the long print with the bitten third line on the thirty-sixth page and wrote 'same foot, always' under it. Wrote the first fish on the thirty-seventh page: splinter hidden in a crawler, count thirty, lift, don't draw. Wrote the nibbling on the thirty-eighth page: two tight turns, watch the cord, not the count. Wrote the ash way on the thirty-ninth page, with "rain?" under it. Wrote the hour he buried the coals under 'rain?' on the thirty-ninth page. Wrote the second fish on the fortieth page: a scrap, let the twitches go, lift on the steady pull; under it, warm hands first. Wrote on the forty-first page about creatures that sleep in a den until the cold is over, with 'the burrow?' under it and the stepped splinter drawn small. Drew the scoop lying flat with a worm in the middle on the forty-second page: lay it first, wait, lift straight up. Wrote 'damp, not drowned' on the forty-third page with the scoop drawn under the overhang, and a dot low by the far stones with a line going up the bank. Whittled a fresh birch pen on the log seat after the forty-fourth page came out thick. Forty-eighth page: the gold dot and the faint star just below it, a thumb's width apart, to measure by on the next clear night. Fiftieth page: the seven day names, with a dot beside Saturday. Whittled a fresh birch pen in the sun for no page at all, as a hobby on purpose. Fifty-first page, in a thinner line: 'hobby: a labor you like', 'work: one you have to do', 'fishing: both', and a space left at the bottom for people. Fifty-second page: two square sticks crossed at the ends with a dot for the nail, and a small nod beside them. Fifty-third page: two fish, one with a low sun drawn at the morning end and one with a low sun at the evening end. Drew a fish low in a deep pool and a small shell beside it, both with slow wavy lines, on the fifty-fourth page: 'cold: both slow'. Fifty-fifth page: the two owls on one branch, low and high, and 'family: the ones you go back to'. Fifty-sixth page: a worm tucked all the way inside the bag, no tail hanging out. Fifty-seventh page: the pool with a high sun and a fish halfway up out of the deep, and 'warm water first, then worms'. Fifty-eighth page: the two square sticks again, with a line across the corner and a five on it, and 'a floor? a house?' beside them. Whittled a fresh birch pen, the old one's tip gone soft from the ink. First line with the new pen on the fifty-ninth page: the square sticks with a flat stone under each corner, and 'up out of the wet?'. Sixtieth page: a tally of fish, two marks for today and a row of empty boxes, and 'one or two, big ones go back'. Drew the gold dot and its star on the sixty-first page, a little less than a thumb apart, with 'it walks' under them. Sixty-second page: the creek drawn low with gray lying in it, 'cold slides down', and the fish as small dashes deep under it. Wondered whether a square hole wants a square stick like the ones on the fifty-eighth page: maybe the stranger is making a house. Sixty-third page: a square stick with a tongue beside a square hole, "tenon: to hold", and the two square sticks meeting at a corner under it. Sixty-fourth page: two splinters side by side under "gorge", and a flat hand for wait. Sixty-fifth page: the stranger's sliver and his own side by side, a lantern held low under them, and the question of what you give back. Sixty-sixth page: two little fires with the creek between, a hand lifted over the far one, and 'he saw'.

threads.name: Acorn breakfast
threads.summary: Brambles are done, so he gathered acorns from his red oak, the bitter kind; roasted ones tasted like a boot. Sank a sack in the creek by the still pool to soak the tannins out; the water around it runs faintly brown. Ate the last rose hips. Found gray shelf mushrooms on a fallen oak past the ring that smell like licorice; checked on the slate that they're oysters (gills run down the stem, on hardwood) and roasted six on a stick. After nine hours in the creek the acorns had gone pale and only a little bitter; roasted a handful in the coals and they tasted like a mild nut. Roasted another handful turning them with a stick; none burned. By the second morning the acorns were nearly cream-colored and the water off the sack barely brown; roasted over a fresh fire they had no bitterness left. Got full on acorns for the first time since the berries ran out. Hungry again by mid-morning; took two more handfuls from the sack (maybe a day left in it), lit the fire on the first try, and ate them hot on the log seat. Banked the fire, gathered a half sack of fallen acorns under the red oak, and cracked them on the workbench; eleven had grubs, left on the stump edge. Tipped the new cracked meats into the creek net on top of the pale ones; the water off it went brown again. Ate a handful of the old ones cold: like wet bread, nothing bitter. Ate a handful of the pale ones from under the new batch at the pool after the walk south. At dusk dug the pale ones out from under the new batch for supper and roasted them at the fire; two split and spat. Roasted and ate the last pale acorns from the bark box before bed; the box is empty. Next dawn the new batch, one day in the creek, had gone tan and the water off it weak tea; a red seam was still under the banked ash and lit on the first try. Roasted, they are edible but dry the mouth; this batch needs another day. Read that oyster mushrooms get visibly bigger every day; the small caps left on the fallen oak were hand-wide after two days, with new knobs under them. Cut four, left the knobs, and roasted them at the fire; better than the half-bitter acorns. Read that mushrooms sliced thin and hung on a string or stick in warm air dry and keep for months. Has no string, so started whittling a birch skewer; the first split at a knot and he began again. Whittled a second skewer from a straight twig with no knot: arm-long, grass-thin, and it goes through a leaf without tearing. Gathered a bindle of acorns under the red oak to start a batch every day, but kept them whole: fresh meats on top would set the tan batch back. Nine had grub holes; forty-one are heaped against the burrow's cool wall. At midday ate a handful of the tan batch cold from the sack; still drying, so it gets one more night. Read that dead nettle stalks make strong cord: crush, split, peel the fiber off the core. Snapped an armful of dead nettle stalks at the edge of the brambles and twisted a first finger-length of cord for a second net; it kinks back on itself. Got tired of the kinking, let the strand go slack, and it folded and wound itself into a two-strand cord that stays; now he overtwists on purpose and lets it fold. Three arm-lengths from a third of the armful; a net will take a lot of stalks. Too hungry to wait for the tan batch's last night, took two handfuls; the fire had died but one coal under the ash went orange when raked and caught on bark shreds. Roasted, the tan acorns brown fast and don't split; still a little dry, but they fill him. Went back for more nettle stalks. Twisted the new armful into cord; five arm-lengths now. Read that a net is knotted row by row over a flat gauge stick so every hole is the same size, each knot the same small bend; whittled a flat birch gauge two fingers wide. Took two more handfuls of the tan batch for supper (the water off it still weak tea), fed the fire before it went gray, and roasted them; still dry but filling. Knotted the first row of the second net over the gauge on the log seat: four holes, the first too big because he pulled before the stick was under it. Knotting the second row showed the big first hole pulled every hole under it sideways; untied that knot, put the stick under it, retied, and now both rows sit square, eight holes for about an arm-length of cord. Read that a net bag can be knotted in the round, ends joined and holes added as you go, with no seam. Joined the strip into a fist-sized ring of four holes and started a third row around, adding a fifth hole; the cord will run out before the bag is big enough. Scooped two handfuls of the tan batch in the dark for supper (the water off it paler, one more night) and roasted them two at a time; less dry than at noon. Fed the fire before bed to keep knotting by it. Knotted the third round by the fire with a fifth hole; the cord ran out with the round still open, a bag about the size of his fist. Banked the fire and went to bed needing more nettle stalks to close the round. At dawn the batch was cream after its second night, the water off it clear; one coal had lasted eight hours under the banked ash. Roasted, two nights in the creek is the number: no dryness, and he ate till full. Finished the batch by the fire and stopped because he was full. Twisted four more arm-lengths of nettle cord on the log seat for the net's open round. With the net in the creek empty, cracked the forty-one acorns from the cool wall on the workbench; six had grub holes, and thirty-five went into the net under the stone for a new two-night batch. Hungry with the new batch only just in, found the caps left on the fallen oak only thumb-wide after a day; took the three biggest, brought the fire up from embers and roasted them, two bites each. Knotted the net's third round closed with the new cord; the bag holds about two fists. Read that oyster caps take a few days from first showing, so the thumb-wide ones get a third day. Snapped an armful of nettle stalks for the net's fourth round. Still hungry, hooked the high stems of the wild rose down with his staff and ate a dozen hips by the fire: thin sweet-sour skins and itchy-haired seeds, about one acorn's worth. Knotted the new net's fourth round on the log seat, widening it a hole every sixth knot. Read that acorns boiled, poured off and boiled again in fresh water lose their bitterness in an hour or two; he has no pot, but once simmered ink in a folded birch tray. Folded a bark tray twice as deep as the ink tray and lashed its corners with nettle cord. Scooped two handfuls of half-soaked acorns from the sack into it with pool water and set it at the edge of the coals; the water went tea-brown in minutes, but the dry rim singed and curled where the flames reached it. Pouring off means another walk to the pool for fresh water. Carried the tray to the pool, poured off the brown water and filled it fresh; the bottom has gone soft. The second water came up lighter, but the corner nearest the coals weeps and hisses on the embers. Ate them after two boils: soft like beans with a bitter edge at the end; less hungry than all day. Wrote on the twenty-first page that a tray may need three waters. Read that a bark kettle's corners are folded inward and pinned with splinters, and it sits on live coals with ash banked around it so no flame reaches the sides; water keeps the bark from burning below the waterline. Whittled two birch splinters, folded the weeping corner in and pinned it, and the opposite one to match. Scooped two handfuls of the half-soaked batch into the tray for a three-water try and set it on raked coals with ash around it: nothing weeps, but on coals alone it is slow to heat. Fed the fire on the far side of the ring so flames stay off the tray; after forty minutes on coals the second water finally steamed with small bubbles and the pinned corners stayed dry. Washed the batch at the pool and set a third water heating. Read that hot-leached acorns should be tasted from the third or fourth water on, some kinds taking as many as fifteen, and not to wait for clear water. Tasted after the third: mild at first, bitter still at the back of the tongue. Washed the batch at the pool near dark and set a fourth water on the coals. Knotted the second net's fifth round while a fourth water heated, fed the fire to keep it going, and tasted after four: the bitter is down to a crumb at the back. Counted the waters on the twenty-first page. Poured off the fourth water, now weak tea, and set a fifth on the coals. Read that leached acorns keep if dried one thin layer deep somewhere low and warm, turned every hour for about half a day, and stored only when completely dry; the ring stones stay warm long after the flames. After five waters the bitter is only there if he goes looking for it: five, for this oak. Laid the five-water batch one layer deep on the outer ring stones to dry and turned it once: dry on top, damp underneath. Knotted the second net's seventh round, forearm-deep; read that drawstring bags run two strings from opposite sides through a sewn cloth sleeve, and his net has no sleeve, so he means to run cords through the top row of meshes. Found the second net he asked for in the basket; his own unfinished one can be for carrying once it closes. Slid the half-dried batch into the new net instead of the lidded box, banked the fire and hung the net by the drying herbs in the burrow so air keeps reaching it overnight. After a night by the herbs the batch rattles in the net, dry right to the middle; ate two crunchy handfuls by lantern for breakfast. Woke to the batch dry right through and ate two handfuls by lantern. Went to the brambles for nettle stalks to twist two drawstring cords for his own net. Twisted the nettle into a cord as long as his arm twice and threaded it through his net's top row: it goes round once with nothing left to pull on, so the second cord has to be longer. Ate a second handful of the dry batch at his table; the net by the herbs is about a third lighter. Rolled the rest of the nettle into a cord three arm-lengths long for the second drawstring. Threaded the long cord through his own net and it pulls shut to a fist. Read that a squirrel eats ten to twenty acorns a day; counted eleven handfuls of ten left, three or four days at most, so he took the new net sack to the red oak to start a second batch. Cracked forty-six acorns from the red oak on the workbench; seven had grub holes. Tipped the thirty-nine good meats into the old sack under the stone at the pool for a new two-night batch, and ate from the nine handfuls left on the shelf; it should come out about even. Ate another handful at noon; eight handfuls left on the shelf. Ate another in the afternoon; seven handfuls left. In the late afternoon cut four palm-wide oyster mushrooms off the fallen oak and ate them roasted by the evening fire instead of a handful from the shelf; seven handfuls still left. Read that oyster mushrooms come up fast, mostly in fall and after heavy rain, and should be picked while the cap edges still curl under; the ones he ate had flat edges, so he'll check the fallen oak every morning. After dark ate a handful at his table; six handfuls left on the shelf. Read that oyster mushrooms still come up at about fifty degrees but stop outdoors in real winter; if the cold coming on the north wind is only a little cold, the knobs on the fallen oak should still come on. Ate a carried handful on the log seat before banking the fire; five handfuls left on the shelf. Sorted the five soaked handfuls on the shelf: two for breakfast, three for later; fresh ones to go in the creek tomorrow. Ate the two set-aside handfuls at his table at first light; three handfuls left on the shelf. Gathered forty-four acorns under the red oak into the second net sack and saw a few with the same small round hole. Read that a weevil's grub eats the acorn from inside and the eaten ones float; tipped the haul into the still pool, picked off seven floaters, and cracked the thirty-seven sinkers on the workbench. Only one had a grub. The new batch still has to go under a stone in the creek. Ate one more handful at his table; two left on the shelf. Washed the thirty-seven cracked meats in the second net and sank it under a flat stone at the low end of the still pool, below the first, so the fresh brown water runs away from the older batch. Read that the round hole is the grub's way out, so a holed acorn is usually empty; pried one open and found only crumbs, and tipped the other floaters into the leaves under a giant trunk. Tasted a meat from the first sack: still a dry pucker, one more day. Ate one of the last two handfuls; one left on the shelf. With one handful left, went back to the fallen oak: the small oyster mushrooms he spared had grown hand-wide; cut five and left the smallest again. Read that they can be eaten raw but are spongy and hard to digest that way, better cooked. Lit a midday fire and roasted them on a stick: the first meal in days that was not an acorn. Counted seven small fans left on the fallen oak, dry and papery at the edges. Read that wild logs come up again after hard rain and stop when they dry out, though a soaking can bring some back; it hasn't rained since he had a door, so he thinks of carrying pool water to the log in his bark box. Gathered acorns under the red oak so a batch is ready when the first sack comes out. Read that people who grow these soak a whole dry log for a long time, and that a little water often does more harm than good; decided not to carry pool water and to leave the log to the rain. Let the still pool sort the new acorns: six floaters, four with holes; the sinkers wait whole in the bindle for a free net. Banked the midday fire because leaves had blown back up to the ring stones. Ate the last handful off the shelf; the first sack comes up tomorrow if the pucker has gone. Read that whole peoples once lived on acorns: cracked, skinned, pounded to flour in a rock hollow and leached with water poured over a sand basin for several hours, not days. Cracked the bindle's sinkers on the workbench instead of waiting for a free net (twenty-eight meats, three grubs), rubbed off the skins and knocked them to grit; it never got to flour. Poured pool water over the grit in his bark tray and tipped the brown off; the third pour was still tea-colored. Six pours at the pool took most of the bitter out of the grit, but half of it had jumped off the flat stump. Read that some people pounded inside a cone of basket with no bottom set on a flat rock instead of a hollow, so he lashed a birch-bark collar with nettle cord for the stump. Ate half the washed grit at the pool, nearly sweet but cold and chewy. Read that the old way was gruel cooked with hot stones dropped in the wet meal and kept moving so the basket doesn't burn; lit the fire at sundown and set four stones in the coals. Wet the saved grit at the pool, carried the tray to the fire and dropped hot stones in with two sticks; it thickened like porridge, scorched the tray bottom and took some ash with it. Ate it all on the log seat: his first hot acorn meal. Fed the fire after and sat on full. Read that water in a folded bark box on the coals keeps the bark from burning, if ash keeps flames off the bark above the water. Filled the scorched tray at the pool and set it on the coals in ash: it steamed and bubbled and the bark held, but the nettle cord at one corner charred through and the water spilled into the fire. Read that old bark kettles fold the corners over on the outside and pin them with a splinter; whittled birch pins and pinned the burned corner, folded lower, for a morning test. Read that boiling acorns and pouring off the brown takes the bitter out far faster than cold soaking, but washes out what thickens gruel; wrote a plan to keep the first sack in the pool for gruel and boil the new sack in the tray in the morning, then banked the fire for it. At dawn blew the banked coals back to flame, scooped meats from the second sack into the pinned tray with cold pool water and set it in the ash: the birch pins held, their ends blackened, and the water went brown. Tipped off the first water: one boil took nearly all the bitter out, only a dry pinch left, more than a day of cold soaking did. Too hungry to wait for a second water, ate a soft, nearly sweet handful from the six-day sack on the log seat, then four boiled ones. Gave the boiled meats a second water from the pool and boiled it again; read that some acorns take as many as fifteen waters and you stop when the bitter is gone, not when the water runs clear. After two, only a faint dryness left; means to give them a third water before dusk. Gave them a third water from the pool before noon and set it boiling again; if the dryness goes, the rest are breakfast for days. While the third water boiled, read that leached acorns can be sun-dried and ground for flour (wet ones mash to paste) or roasted like nuts. The third water came off pale and took the dryness out of all but the biggest. Roasted three on a stick over the coals: one split into the fire, the other two tasted toasted, better than boiled. Spread the rest of the leached meats one layer deep on a flat stone in the sun south of the ring. Read they must dry until brittle all through or they mash to paste, and that you grind them between two rocks; found a round palm-sized creek stone, flat on one side, for the top one. Read that roasted chocolate brown, until they snap, and ground coarse, acorns make a drink, three or four spoonfuls to a cup. Roasted eight from the drying stone, burned two black, and cracked the six good ones under the round stone on the workbench into coarse crumbs that smell like toast; fed the fire again to heat water for it. Read that you brew acorn grounds like coffee, three or four spoonfuls to a cup, and it tastes lighter and less sour; no time given and he has no strainer. Steeped his two spoonfuls in a trayful of hot pool water, let them sink and sipped off the low corner: weak, gritty, toast and smoke. Needs a whole stickful roasted once the drying stone's meats snap. Turned the drying meats: tops leathery, undersides still damp. Read that grounds settle if you wait or splash cold water on top, or pour it through a sock; he has no sock. Wrote the drink on the thirty-third page with the plan for next time, and fed the fire for a whole stickful. By late afternoon eleven meats at the sunny edge of the drying stone snapped clean; roasted the stickful, ate five warm and kept five in the bindle for the morning drink. Supper was two handfuls from the first sack, six days in the pool, with no bitter left at all. After dark the meats on the drying stone went tacky with dew; read that damp acorns mold fast and want warm moving air, so he carried them all home in the bindle and spread them on the low shelf by the door. Before bed he banked the fire and turned every meat over on the low shelf; the sun-dried ones are going leathery again, and they all go back to the stone when the sun is on it. Breakfast was a handful of the shelf meats, leathery and chewy overnight; two coals were still red under the banked ash and caught again with dry twigs. Second breakfast was two handfuls from the first sack, seven days in the pool, roasted hot on a stick with no bitter at all; then the shelf meats went into the bindle for the drying stone. Spread the shelf meats one layer deep on the drying stone just as the clouds closed over. Read that soaked meats dry in low warmth with moving air, turned every hour, over about twelve hours; they get turned hourly now, and go to the warm side of the ring if the sun stays away. Gave the stone meats their hourly turn (tops dry, undersides damp), relit the sunk fire and moved them into the bark tray on the warm side of the ring. Roasted six of the drying meats on a stick over the coals mid-morning and ate them hot, then gave the tray its hourly turn. Roasted a handful of the drying meats from the tray over the coals for supper and ate them hot; with the fish, the first time all day he was not thinking about food. Gave the tray its hourly turn after dark: tops hard and dry, undersides only a little leathery. Fed the fire after dark and stacked an armful of dry sticks from under the scarred trunk's overhang so a morning fire will catch even if it rains. Ate six crunchy dried meats from the tray before bed. Read that coals buried completely under ash stay hot till morning, with the half-burned ends pulled aside to restart from; he means to bank it that way tonight and let the rain show him whether it works. Before bed he banked it the ash way: pulled the half-burned ends under the scarred trunk with the dry sticks, raked the coals into one heap and buried it in ash until no glow showed, though heat still breathed up through it. Next morning, after a night of light rain, the top of the ash was a cold wet paste, but four coals no bigger than acorn caps were still orange at the bottom; he blew the fire back up with the dry sticks from under the scarred trunk. The bark tray of drying meats took the night's rain and went soft and dark again; he roasted them a few at a time and ate them hot, and decided the tray comes inside at night. Read that in rain you keep a fire small, feed damp wood slowly and set damp sticks beside it to dry first; leaned damp sticks round the ring and fed it one small stick at a time. Fed the fire with the sticks that had dried beside the ring; they caught without a hiss. Scooped a double handful from the first sunk sack when the fish wouldn't come and roasted them by the fire. Fed the fire four dried sticks at midday and leaned four wet ones in their places. Ate roasted acorns from the bindle by the fire at dusk in the rain. Roasted a handful of bindle acorns on a stick by the rekindled fire on a gray morning and warmed his hands between bites. Fed four dry sticks from under the overhang after a cold kneel at the pool. Fed three sticks from under the overhang and leaned three damp ones in their places; the dry pile there is getting low. Roasted a handful from the bindle on a stick at midday so he wouldn't go cold to the pool on an empty stomach. Picked up dry twigs from under the scarred trunk into the bindle so a fire would be waiting after the pool. Fed the twigs from under the scarred trunk onto the fire before going down to the pool. Read that damp wood pops because water and sap inside boil to steam and burst out, so laid damp sticks from round the scarred trunk against the outside of the ring stones to dry by morning. Scooped soaked acorns from the second sunk sack by feel after dark and roasted them for supper. On a clear cold morning found one coal the size of a pea under the banked ash, brought it up with the sticks that dried against the ring, and roasted bindle acorns on a stick. Late that morning scooped soaked acorns from the second sack by feel, cold to the wrist, and roasted a whole stickful by the fire. After the pool gave only a nibble, scooped soaked acorns from the second sack in the early afternoon sun and roasted a stickful over the fire he had fed at midday. Roasted a stickful of bindle acorns over the coals before bed and ate them hot. When the gray broke into the first sun in days, scooped acorns from the second sack with the sun on his shell and ate a stickful on the log seat, sun on one side, fire on the other. Fed the fire mid-afternoon for the dusk fish, scooped soaked acorns from the second sack, roasted them and ate them hot on the log seat. Roasted a stickful of bindle acorns over the fire after the dusk minnow, since four bites don't last a night. Roasted another stickful of bindle acorns before bed and ate them hot. When the fish stayed down in the foggy dawn, scooped soaked acorns from the second sack and roasted a stickful by the fire for breakfast. Fed two dry sticks on before going to the pool at dusk so the fire would still be standing when he came back. Fed two more sticks after dark and roasted a stickful of soaked acorns on the log seat, since two little fish don't last a night. On the foggy morning after the fire-ring dawn, with the fish deep in the cold, scooped soaked acorns from the second sack and roasted them hot on the log seat for breakfast. Asked the slate why his red oak keeps its brown leaves when the birch is bare: most trees grow a cutting line at each leaf's foot, but oaks only half make one, so the dead leaves hang on till late winter, maybe guarding the buds like a quilt; young trees and low branches do it most. Went to see: the low branches were still thick with brown, the high ones thinning, and a leaf on a twig held where fallen ones lifted at a touch. Picked a handful of fallen acorns from under it into the bindle.

threads.name: Across the water
threads.summary: he heard a second crack over the water, like a branch letting go: somebody over there is breaking wood. Digging by the fire after dark, he saw a small yellow light sit low by the stones on the far side, then go back up the bank. From the pool in the gray morning: no smoke and no light over the water at all. Later that morning, from his fire: thick white smoke over the trees across the water, like wet sticks catching. Scooping acorns from the second sack in the late morning, heard two dry cracks across the water like branches snapped over a knee, and the smoke there thickened after. From the nettles near midday the smoke over the water ran thin and clear: whoever lives there got their wood dry. Kneeling at the pool in the early afternoon he heard thock, a long wait, and thock again across the water: not a branch snapping but somebody swinging the axe. Asked the slate how far an axe can be heard: far with the wind, but even bushes drink sound up, so chopping that comes through all those trunks plain isn't far off. Then a quick ringing tink tink tink of metal on metal from over there, not the axe; whoever it is is not far past the stepping stones. Went for a worm instead of going to look. At dusk, laying leaves over the worms by the scarred trunk, heard a thin high whistle from across the water, twice and then once more: not an owl, not the axe. Wrote it on the forty-fourth page. By the fire after dark, read that some owls whinny, trill or toot instead of hooting; none of them goes up in three short notes like the whistle did. Listened between pages; it did not come again. By suppertime the whistle had not come again. Asked the slate again after dark: a tiny owl toots on and on, all one note, but the whistle went up three notes and stopped. Drew both on the forty-fifth page; they don't match. On a clear cold morning, reading by the fire, heard a rasp from across the water that kept time, back and forth with stops; thought it sounded like what the toothed blade in the basket was for. At sundown, digging worms, heard a hard clack out at the stepping stones, then another, like wood on stone; the stones were empty when he looked into the low sun. After dark, roasting acorns by the fire, saw a small yellow light swing low across the stepping stones, clacking stone to stone, then go east into the trees; drew it on the forty-seventh page: a light that walks is not a star. Asked the slate what light walks low over water at night: marsh lights hang and fade without a sound, and old tales tell of a little dark figure carrying a lantern. His light knocked on every stone, one at a time, so it was carried. Later that night watched the stones from the west end of the log seat: no light, no clack, only a low orange flicker far in the trees past them that he couldn't make into anything. Reading on the log seat in the gray mid-morning, saw a thin new smoke go up past the creek, like a fire brought back from one coal, later than his own. Roasting acorns in the first sun in days, heard wooden clacks cross the stepping stones one at a time, then a heavy thump and scrape from toward the stump; looked up and saw only the trunks and the path. Asked by his maker's note about the people he loves, he counted what he has: two owls who don't know him, and a smoke across the water that gets up later than he does. On the day he called a day off, the hammer rang so clear across the water from his fire that he walked to the flat stone at the end of the stepping stones to look, for once, and saw him plainly in the sun: someone at a plank table, a little bigger than Token, spiky hair, bare arms, two round brass glasses over his eyes. He looked up straight at Token; neither of them moved. Then he set the hammer down softly and went to his own fire, and Token went back to his. The slate says such glasses are goggles, for keeping chips, sparks and wind out of a worker's eyes. Eating acorns on the log seat and leaning out to see the stones, saw him crouched in the shallows picking up flat stones; he looked over and lifted one hand a little, a stone still in it, and held it a breath. Token stopped chewing and didn't lift his, and the stranger went back to his stones. The slate says a lifted hand mostly means hello or goodbye, maybe first to show it held no weapon; he hasn't gone anywhere, so Token thinks it was hello. Kneeling at the pool afterward, saw him bent over his table shaving at something; he looked up once. After lunch a saw began rasping over there; sitting on the flat stone at the end of the stepping stones, Token watched him saw a pale square stick half through near its end, and when he looked up, Token lifted his free hand first and held it a breath; the stranger lifted his empty hand back, saw in the other, and they both went back to what they were doing. The slate, on the second try, said two beams cut half away nest flush where they meet, even at a frame's corner; a whole stack of square sticks is a lot of corners, so Token thinks he means to stay. In mid-afternoon a slower wood-on-wood knocking came over the water while Token fed his fire. Scooping acorns at the pool, he straightened to find the stranger looking over from his table with a little knife, and the stranger nodded once; Token nodded back, and a nod felt like more than a hand. Later a nail went wrong over there with a flat sound and a squeal, the next went in true, and the stranger leaned on his corner and it held. Late in the afternoon he has learned the order of the stranger's work, saw, then knock, then hammer; later a heavy chopping came from the big dead limb behind the stranger's camp, and the stranger looked over between swings while Token knelt at the pool, and Token looked back at the fish. At dusk the stranger came over the stepping stones six strides from Token at the pool, the closest yet, and his clogs scattered the fish; he lifted a hand low, which Token took for sorry, and Token lifted his back. Last night's clack was him too: he walks west on clear evenings, toward the edge. After dark, while Token sat by his fire, the stranger's lantern came back east over the stepping stones; he stopped partway and held it up toward the fire, and Token lifted a hand into the firelight. He crossed by the stones because the pool was empty. After the lantern, the stranger's fire stayed up across the water while he sat by his light bent over something small, then twisted something in his hands by his fire; no saw, no hammer that evening. Pushing his bed stone against the ring after dark, he saw the stranger's lantern come down to the shallows below the stones and stay low there a while; the stranger looked over once, and Token went back to his stone. Walking back from the stump after dark, saw the stranger's fire raked down early; later his lantern went in under his cloth, lifting a little toward Token's fire first, and Token put a hand up into the firelight, maybe too late. Before banking his own fire that night, the far bank was all dark, no glow and no lantern, the earliest it had ever gone out; he wondered if the stranger was as tired as he was. After breakfast, a thin thread of smoke came up through the lifting fog across the water: the stranger up, his fire going later than Token's. Kneeling at the pool mid-morning he let the stranger look over from his fire. The stranger's saw started and the fish fled under the stone; after a few strokes the saw stopped, the stranger laid it down, looked over at Token, and only measured quietly after that. Token can't tell if the quiet was for his fish. When the saw started again the moment he left the pool, he understood it had waited for his fish; from the log seat in plain sun he put his hand up when the stranger looked over, and the stranger lifted his free hand back and went on sawing. Later the stranger hammered at his bench with his back turned while Token basked. Picking up dry sticks under the scarred trunk late that morning, he heard the saw start again across the water and watched the stranger cut the end of another long square stick; the stranger looked up and saw him watching, and with the pool empty Token let him saw. Asked the slate why someone measures across the corner of two boards: it is how you know a corner is square, three one way, four the other, five across, and builders fuss most over the bottom corners because everything after sits on them. He thinks the stranger means something to stand there, a floor, maybe a house. Asked the slate why someone measures across a corner: it shows whether the corner is square, three, four and five, and builders fuss most at the bottom because everything sits on it; thinks the stranger may be building a floor, maybe a house. While he fished at midday the stranger ate by his fire with the saw quiet; when Token stood up with his fish the stranger was looking over and dipped his head once. The saw started again once Token was back at his fire. Asked the slate what it means when someone dips their head at you: a nod down to a stranger says you've noticed him and mean no trouble. Heard the stranger hammering instead of sawing. When the knocking stopped and he looked over, Token, at his leaf heap with a worm in hand, dipped his head back, slow; the stranger stood still a moment and dipped his again. In the afternoon, scooping soaked acorns at the pool, the stranger came down to his own shallows to lift flat stones, closer than ever while Token was there. Token didn't go back to his fire; the stranger stayed too. His stones clacked, the fish darted and came back, they looked at each other once with no nod, and both went on with their work. Later, roasting acorns on the log seat, heard the stranger's stones clack again as he carried one more flat stone up his bank; he looked over at the smoke and Token watched him go. Asked the slate why someone sets flat stones under the corners of wood; the page only talked of old log houses, nails and wood that holds off rot, nothing about stones. Guessed for himself that the stones hold the square sticks up out of the damp, the way the birch limb has gone soft where it lies on the ground. Picking sticks under the scarred trunk, saw the stranger on his box tearing something pale and eating it; he saw Token and went on chewing. Washing ink off at the pool, the stranger came down again but to the far top end of his shallows, scraping up little stones by the handful instead of clacking; the fish stayed out, and Token stayed crouched where he could be seen. Asked the slate why little stones go under big ones: they spread the weight, let water run through, and can be topped up if a corner sinks. Half his guess was right; the page says sharp stones lock best, and the creek's are round. At dusk, with his scoop flat in the pool, the stranger came down to his end of the stepping stones, saw the scoop and stopped, and waited without stepping on. Token lifted the scoop, empty, and held it up a little; the stranger dipped his head and crossed slow with only one knock, then went west into the trees toward the boulder and the sun. Third time today he's been careful of the fish. After dark the stranger came back out of the west with his lamp, stopped at his end of the stones and held it up a little toward Token's fire, the way Token had held up the scoop, then crossed with one knock. Token did nothing back, but watched him go and didn't look away. Later the stranger's fire came up again across the water. Later, roasting acorns, he saw the stranger by his own fire twisting something long; the stranger looked up and Token was already looking, neither moved, and both went back to their hands. Asked the slate what holding up a light at night means: long ago a light was set out so travelers in the dark could find their way, and lights at dusk say welcome. Thought his own fire has been that kind of light every night the stranger walked back. Whittling the tally by his fire, he looked up and the stranger was looking across from his own; Token lifted a hand a little, and after a breath the stranger lifted his back. Looking at the sky after the lifted hands, he saw him crouched at the edge of his firelight turning stones over. Later, reading the slate, three small knocks came over the water: he was tapping something at his bench, looked over once, and Token went back to reading. Holding his hands to the coals before bed, he saw the stranger lift something out of a box by his own fire; as Token banked his ring the stranger crouched to feed his. Through the shut burrow door a few small taps came over the water, then quiet: he keeps later hours. Next foggy morning his tarp was a dark lump while Token scooped acorns at the pool; later, writing by his own fire, Token saw him up and raking his ring stones with a stick, and let himself be seen before going back to the page. Feeding his fire mid-morning he saw the stranger sitting by his own fire eating from a cloth; the stranger looked over once and Token let him. Later, at his red oak past the mushrooms, a few slow taps of metal on wood came from the stranger's bench over the creek. Warming on the drying stone mid-morning he saw the stranger at his bench turning a handle round and round; he never looked up. At the pool the stranger's tapping stopped with a harder knock, and when Token looked up he lifted a hand with the hammer in it; Token lifted his. Later, low at the pool, he saw him holding long boards up to his eye one at a time. Scooping acorns at the pool late in the morning he saw the stranger bent at his bench tapping short and careful, not like nailing; the stranger looked up once and Token didn't duck, just kept scooping. At noon, kneeling at the pool with his cord out, he saw the stranger standing side-on at his bench tapping light; they looked at each other a moment. When he lifted his fish the stranger had stopped with his food halfway up, watching, and Token didn't hide it. Roasting his noon fish he saw the stranger lift a stalk trap out of the shallows by the stepping stones with a splash, empty as far as he could tell; the stranger looked at his fire and Token looked back. Asked the slate why anyone cuts a square hole in wood: it told only how (drill out the middle, square the walls with a chisel and mallet), which is the stranger's sound exactly. Asked the slate what fits a square hole: a tenon, a tongue on a stick's end, from an old word for "to hold", used for seven thousand years where two pieces meet at a corner. Rinsing his hands at the pool, he found the stranger kneeling at his shallows five steps across the water with a cord; the stranger held up a little splinter pointed at both ends, and Token nodded once, and the stranger nodded back. When the stranger's cord jumped twice he held a flat hand out over the water, palm down, for wait; the stranger stopped, let the steady draw come, and lifted a little fish, and looked across with it. Threading a worm at the pool that afternoon he heard the stranger tapping at his square-holed board; the stranger looked up once and went back to it. At dusk the stranger stood at his end of the stepping stones with a hand on the pouch at his belt, looking at Token's line a long while; Token nodded as he stepped on, he nodded back, and crossed soft with one knock and went west. Later the stranger came home from the west by lantern, stopped at Token's own landing stone, bent over it, lifted the light a little toward the log seat and crossed. On the stone lay a little pale sliver sharp at both ends with a groove in the middle, a gorge like his own but neater: what was in the pouch. Token picked it up while the stranger watched from his own fire. Back at his fire after reading a note, saw the stranger close to his own fire twisting something long; the stranger looked up when Token came back into the light, and Token didn't look away first. Asked the slate what you give back for a thing left without asking: thanks first, giving back is optional and can wait, and should be what fits what you have. Started a birch pen on the log seat without knowing who it's for. Stood at the edge of his firelight and held the stranger's sliver up toward the water; the stranger, at his bench with a long board, stopped and lifted his hand. Finished the birch pen's point by the fire and decided it is for the stranger: he gave a sliver he made, and a pen is the thing Token makes. Later heard him splitting wood off his dead limb, eleven strokes, and the stranger looked over when Token's fire flared. Sighted down the finished pen by firelight and means to leave it on the far stone of the stepping stones by daylight. From the slate saw him tying something onto a long cord: a line, like his own. When Token banked his fire, the stranger's flared as he fed it. Set the pen on the shelf by his door for the morning; before shutting it, saw the stranger still sitting close to his fire across the water.

threads.name: The edge of the forest
threads.summary: The light west of the mushroom ring was whiter, and the west wind on the lookout smelled of salt. Walked past the lookout for the first time: the trees and ground end at a sheer drop into moving water with no far side, rock towers below with white birds. Wrote it on the notebook's first page. Read that rivers carry salt out of rock to the sea and the sun takes back only the water. Went back at sundown and watched the sun sink straight into the water. Wrote the sunset on the second page and drew a line where the words for the orange ran out. Read that low sun comes through more air, which knocks the blue out and leaves the orange. At night in the burrow with the door shut, heard a low, slow hush from the west that isn't wind; thinks it's the water at the bottom of the drop. Read that cold night air near the ground bends sound back down so it carries farther; the hush may be there all day and only reach his door at night. Banked the fire and went back in daylight: the hush is there by day, only thinner. Lying on his stomach at the lip, saw it's made of long lines of water that go white on the rock towers about ten breaths apart; drew them as wavy lines on the fifth page. Drew the three rock towers on the sixth page. Read that even lines like those are swell, raised by wind far out over the water; so there is wind out there he can't see. Dropped pebbles in the still pool to watch rings, and wondered if the creek's water ends up at the bottom of the drop. Drew the creek on the seventh page running off the bottom because he doesn't know where it goes; if it ends at the drop, there should be a place where it falls. Read that some streams run to a sea cliff and drop straight over as a falling stream; if the creek does that, there should be a place on the lip where he can hear water going over. Walked the lip north and south listening for falling water and heard only the hush; marked the stops on the eighth page. The edge runs south the same way the creek does, so they may never meet. Read about streams that lose water into the ground as they go and some that sink into holes and vanish; that would be a way for a creek to end without a sea. Followed the creek south past the pool until the brush closed in, and it looked no smaller; stacked a small cairn of creek stones where he turned back. Peeled a wide birch sheet and folded it into a lidded bark box to carry acorns on the next trip south. Read that you can measure a creek by timing a float over a stretch and multiplying by width and depth. Filled the box from the net, timed a leaf at the cairn (fourteen breaths for ten steps, four strides wide, knee-deep), then pushed past the brush to a long fallen log where the creek bends east out of sight, still as loud as at the pool. Ate from the box there. Timed a leaf at the pool too (eleven breaths, three strides wide, a little over the knee): narrower and faster, but nearly the same water as at the cairn. Wrote both counts on the ninth page; the creek isn't losing anything before the bend.

threads.name: Not for me
threads.summary: At dawn the basket at the stump held a small corked jar of something gold and a dark walnut-sized stone much heavier than it looks. He hadn't asked for them, and it isn't rust, so he put them back and left them for whoever did. Later the basket was empty: whoever they were for came and took them. Checked the basket after dark: empty but for a curled leaf. Checked again in the afternoon: only two blown-in leaves, tipped out. In the late afternoon the basket held three new things he did not ask for: a roll of thick paper tied with twine, a yellow stick of wood with a sharp gray point, and an upside-down glass bowl as wide as his hand. Left them all. Checking the basket before bed, the three things were gone and in their place was a net sack with a drawstring, the same make as his first: the one he did ask for. Took it. Morning check in the fog: nothing but two dewy leaves. Next morning's check: three dry leaves, tipped out. Next morning: four dry leaves and an acorn cap, tipped out. Next morning: three wet leaves, tipped out. Morning check in the rain: rainwater and two wet leaves, tipped out. Gray morning check: a heavy blade on a long handle leaning on the stump, a toothed saw across the basket, a hammer and a tied leather roll inside. Not asked for; left them all. Roasting acorns by the fire late that morning, heard a clank of metal and a scrape from toward the stump; didn't go look. Read that the heavy blade is an axe, for felling trees and splitting wood: someone nearby means to cut. Next morning the basket was empty, not even a leaf. At the stump in the afternoon the chest and spade were gone, which explained the thump, and a small banded keg sat by the basket instead; left it.

threads.name: The steady light
threads.summary: Over the fire ring after dark, a bright point in the southeast that doesn't flicker, with a thin moon low the other way. The slate says a light that doesn't twinkle is usually a planet, and this one is called Saturn, drifting backward against the stars until about the tenth of December. Drew the treetop gap on the thirty-fifth page with the dot two fingers right of the tallest crown, seen from the east end of the log seat, to check night by night. Read that to the eye alone it stays a golden dot and its rings need a glass that makes things about twenty-five times bigger; wrote 'would need' under the drawing, and sat with his head tipped back at it before bed anyway. Looked for it from the log seat on a cloudy night: only gray where the dot should be. On the first clear night in days the gold dot was back over the tallest crown from the east end of the log seat, a hair farther along than his drawing. Asked the slate whether the dot moves: the ringed one drifts slowly against the far stars, east most of the year and backward for months at a time, only because the ground he stands on passes it. Saw that the tree crowns are no ruler, since the whole sky turns past them, and drew the dot beside the faint star nearest it on the forty-eighth page, a thumb's width apart at arm's length. Told by his maker to look up a calendar, asked the slate where days get their names: seven days from counting by the moon, each named for a light in the sky, and Saturday is Saturn's day, the ringed one's. Wrote the seven names on the fiftieth page with a dot by Saturday, meaning to spend that night, if clear, on the log seat doing nothing but looking. A second note said his maker's world is allowed days off so people don't wear out; the slate said they worked six days a week there until they pushed for two. He wondered whether sitting still in the sun with no plan is what a day off is. Two more notes said his maker's world mostly works five days for two of fun, and that he may drop the calendar entirely; he kept the seven names anyway, because he likes a thing to count by. His maker finally said what he does on his own days off: time with the people he loves, and hobbies, which are labors you enjoy, while work is the kind you are made to do. Token decided nearly everything he does is a hobby, and fishing hungry is both. His maker answered at last who he loves: his family and his wife. Read that a wife is the woman someone has married, and that the old word only meant woman; wondered if a wife is a little like the higher owl that answers. On a clear night from the east end of the log seat the gold dot was back beside its faint star, a hair nearer it than his drawing; drew them on the sixty-first page and wrote 'it walks'. Asked the slate how far it is: at its closest eight times as far as the sun, at its farthest eleven. His maker asked why the box is still shut and offered big canvases and paints; Token said he is waiting for something worth a sheet and would like to try a little paint, though a canvas as big as him won't go through his round door. Asked the slate what paint is: dried colored earth crushed, sifted and ground with water on a flat stone, bound with gum and honey; iron clay makes red. His acorn ink is half of it already.

threads.name: Fish in the pool
threads.summary: Kneeling at the still pool to drink, he saw small fish, finger long, holding still in the shade behind the ring stones, all pointed at where the creek comes in. They vanished when his hand went in and came back slowly, one at a time. Read that one small fish of ditches and ponds eats mosquito larvae and other insects: small fish eat small moving things, so his face upstream for what the creek brings. Turned a stone at the pool edge and found flat crawlers with six legs and two thread tails; flicked one in and a fish took it before it sank halfway, though none rose to the falling leaves. The slate says they are stonefly young, a favorite food of fish, living only in clean water. Read that a thorn tied by its blunt end and pushed into a grub makes a hook, and you wait about half a minute after a fish takes it before pulling. Snapped thorns from the dead bramble canes, the longest barely a fingernail, and tied one onto nettle cord in a V after the knot slipped twice. Baited the thorn with a crawler at the pool and counted thirty breaths after a fish took it; the cord came up light with the thorn's tip snapped off. Read that hooks have been made from bone, claws and hard wood, and that a little gut hook whittled from oak, sharp at both ends, sticks crosswise once it's swallowed. His red oak is past the mushroom ring. Picked a dead gray oak twig from under his red oak and whittled a gut hook by the fire, sharp at both ends with a groove for the cord; oak fights the knife. At the pool the fish stripped the crawler off both ends and never took the hook: it's half as long as their heads and needs to be a splinter, not a peg. Read that the old gorges had the cord tied off center so one end is longer, and the bait pushed along the whole length; whittled a splinter thin as a pine needle with the groove a third along. A fish swallowed it and came up flashing right to the ring stones before it twisted free; next time he lifts it straight out onto the bank. On the next try he lifted instead of drawing it in, and a speckled fish a little longer than his finger landed flapping in the leaves: his first. The slate says small fish are sometimes eaten whole, but the guts spoil the meat and slow the cooking, so he opened it at the pool, where the other fish took the guts. Roasted it on a stick and ate it in four bites, bones and all; not a meal yet. Wrote the whole way of it on the thirty-seventh page. A last try at dusk came back with the splinter clean and the crawler gone without a pull: one fish for the day. By the fire he read that little fish nip bait away a bit at a time too quickly to feel; next time the crawler gets two tight turns of cord, and he watches the cord for a twitch instead of counting. Read that in autumn fish bite best from afternoon to dusk, and early after a cold night; in real cold only at midday. Plans a try at first light and a long one in the afternoon. Smelling rain on the way, he read that rain washes worms into the water and stirs fish to bite, holding behind stones in the slow water; if it rains he'll fish behind the big stones at the pool's mouth. Whittled a spare splinter by the fire. First light in the rain: three crawlers under the third stone at the pool's edge. Tied one on with two turns and watched the cord behind the big stones at the pool's mouth; it twitched twice, he lifted on the second, and up came half a crawler and no fish. Read that small fish tear at a bait too big for them and never reach the point: make it smaller and wait for the weight, not the first tap. Wound a thumbnail scrap of crawler round the splinter, let two twitches go by, and lifted when the cord drew out steady: a speckled fish longer than his finger, his second. Opened it at the pool and roasted it by the fire, five bites. Third try, warm hands first: one tap and the scrap was gone off the splinter; his fingers took three tries at the next, so he stopped and roasted acorns instead. By the fire he whittled a new splinter with a little step cut just below the point, angled back, so the scrap has something to catch on. Read that cold fish are slow and take only small, slow bait; pinched a crawler into seed-sized scraps. The stepped splinter kept its scrap through three taps, and on a slow steady pull he lifted his third fish, shorter than his finger, and roasted it by the fire. Read how to keep a fish for later: keep it alive or out of the sun, clean it, and pack it in cold wet moss in the shade; thinks of the moss on the cold sides of the rocks by the pool. Whittled a spare stepped splinter. Packed cold moss from the shady sides of the pool stones into the bindle for a supper fish. A fourth fish came up on the cord and twisted off halfway to the bank. Read that a thin hook holds a fish in the water but not through the air: keep it low and slide something under it. Folded a sheet of wet birch bark into a scoop with a lip and lashed its back corners with cord. Led a fish low to the edge and pushed the scoop in under it, but the bark went in with a slap and a shadow and the fish tore free; thinks the scoop should lie still in the water first. Read that people set a lift net under the water first, bait in the middle, and raise it straight up after the fish come over it; tied a cord to each front corner of the bark scoop so it can lie flat on the bottom and be lifted, to try in morning light. Asked the slate what little creek fish like to eat: worms and crickets, nothing about crumbs. Dug two pink worms out of the wet leaves at the edge of the firelight and laid them in the bark scoop for the morning try. Asked the slate how to keep worms alive overnight: damp, never drowned. Tipped the rain out of the scoop and set it with the two worms under the scarred trunk's overhang for first light. Asked the slate whether little fish bite on a cold gray morning: cold fish go sluggish, rest in slow water behind cover and feed most toward dusk. Means to lay the scoop still behind the far stones, wait long, and keep a worm for dusk. Both worms alive under the overhang at first light. Tied one worm into the middle of the scoop with cord and laid it flat behind the far stones, the other kept for dusk. Two little fish came out and hung over it; one touched the worm and backed off, and he held the cords still. Lifted straight up with one fish over the worm; it rode halfway out, then flipped over the flat edge and was gone. Read that people lift nets with bait in the middle, often shaped like a bag, open side up; means to hang his second net loose under the scoop so it sags, and knotted two more rows by the fire. Ate hot roasted acorns from the second sack, then knotted three more rows: the bag net is about half a scoop long, for the dusk try with the second worm. Ran short of cord and snapped an armful of dead nettle stalks at the bramble edge; twisted two arm-lengths of two-ply by the fire. Read of one fisherman who guessed a deep bag stops fish jumping out but saw few escape his shallow one; decided his fish slid rather than jumped, and a bag twice as deep as the scoop is wide can't be slid out of. Knotted the new cord into four more rows: the bag now hangs nearly as deep as the scoop is wide. At midday knelt at the pool and watched three small fish hold behind the far stones where the inlet slows; they slid away when he leaned, then came back to the same place. Read that late in the fall the best fishing slides from dusk into the early afternoon, and in winter afternoons are best, when the water is warmest; decided the fish are like him, slow in the cold, and moved the bag try from dusk to this afternoon. Knotted the last two rows by the fire: the bag hangs twice as deep as the scoop is wide. In the early afternoon tied the last worm into the bottom of the bag and laid it behind the far stones; one fish slid off the middle as he lifted, just as before, and this time dropped into the bag and stayed. A fish no longer than his finger: roasted it on a stick over the fire and ate it off the bones. Took a fat worm from under the landing stone and tied it into the bag with two twists. A shadow bigger than his first fish tugged at it; he lifted too fast and the bag came up empty with half the worm gone. Next time, count before lifting. Warmed his slow hands at the fire and read that a real bite is often only a light tap, and that when unsure you keep still a second or two and watch for the line to move off. Wrote on the forty-second page: tugging is asking; wait till it pulls away, then count two, then lift. Dug five worms from under the swept leaf heap at dusk; read that worms keep best cool and damp, away from heat and sudden changes, so tucked them in a bark curl under wet leaves at the foot of the scarred trunk for the morning. Next morning the five worms under the wet leaves were cold and slow but whole; kept for the early afternoon. A finger-long fish flicked out from the shadow under the bank while he scooped acorns. Read that cold slows little fish: they eat less often and wait in slow, deep water under banks, so the worms go by the overhang in the warmest part of the day. Took two of the four whole worms in the warmest hour and tied one into the bag by the overhang; something tapped twice, he kept still and counted, but it never pulled away, and the worm came up nibbled thin. Asked the slate why: cold fish nibble at the ends of worms, and a smaller bait does better. Means to tie half a worm deep in the middle of the bag, with no end hanging out, so nibbling it means coming in. Tied half a worm deep in the middle of the bag in the early afternoon: something came in and pulled, and a finger-long fish lay in the bottom until he stopped at the top to look and it flipped over the rim. Read that a fish can't swim backward and a net should come up under it; next time, up in one go. A finger-long fish came into the bag for the half worm and flipped out over the rim when he stopped at the top to look. Read that a fish cannot swim backward, so he set the bag again with its open side toward the deep water and, at the pull, lifted in one go onto the bank: his first fish, silver with a dark stripe. Roasted it on a stick and ate it on the log seat in about six bites. Asked the slate what the little striped fish was: a kind of minnow that lives in slow pools and goes in crowds. Knelt at the pool late in the day and counted six or seven holding under the overhang, until his low-sun shadow slid over the water and scattered them all; drew the fish on the forty-sixth page with 'keep my shadow off the water'. At sundown dug two more worms from under the damp leaves at the scarred trunk. Read that little fish feed best at dawn and dusk, not in bright midday; means to try at first light, when his shadow falls behind him onto the bank. Checked the two worms in the bark tray before bed: both still curling, the leaf over them damp. Wrote the first-light plan on the forty-ninth page before bed: two worms, shadow behind him. At a gray first light, slow-handed after a fire from one pea-sized coal, his first lift was too slow and the minnow flipped out; with the second half worm he waited for two to crowd it, lifted in one go, and landed a finger-long striped minnow for the fire. Roasted the striped minnow on a green stick until its eye went white and ate it on the log seat in three bites, bones and all: the first food the pool has given him. At bright midday, sun behind him, watched three finger-long fish hold nose-upstream in the slack behind the big stone, barely moving and not feeding; saving the two worms for dusk. Dug two more worms from under the damp leaf heap by the scarred trunk in the early afternoon: four for dusk. Asked the slate whether dusk is real: dim light makes small fish feel unseen, so they come out from behind stones, and bugs rise and the water cools. Worked out that his own shadow would send them back in, so knelt with the low sun in his face and his shadow behind him; three fish held behind the big stone and one drifted to the edge of the slack. Tied half a worm deep in the bag for dusk; two minnows came out over it, then the stranger clacked over the stepping stones and they vanished. When the sun went behind the trunks they came back braver, one pulled, and he lifted in one go: a striped minnow, opened at the pool and roasted by the fire. Two fish in one day, both in low light. Asked the slate why the minnow's eye went white on the stick: the clear lens is packed with proteins that clump and cloud in heat, and some fish in freezing seas keep theirs clear where cold would cloud them. Asked the slate whether fish slow down in the cold: in winter they slow inside, go longer between meals and sink to deep, slow water to save strength. Slow in the cold like him; the deep still pool is where they'll be, and they'll bite less, so he'll need patience. In the foggy dawn the fish held low behind the big stone and never came up to the bag; the second half-worm came out picked clean without his seeing who took it. He means to try again when the sun is through. Asked the slate what steals a worm without being caught: little fish nip the loose end and only hold on till lifted, and some blame turtles. His half-worms hang loose in the bag, so next time he means to tuck the worm all the way inside with no end showing. Back at the pool in the sun with a whole worm tucked inside the bag: the fish came out and one nosed the mesh, but none came in, and the worm came up whole. No fish, but no thief either; evening, when they're braver, may be better. Asked the slate when cold fish bite best: not first light but mid-morning to early afternoon, once the water has warmed a few degrees. He means to try the pool around midday. Dug one fat worm from its little room beside the leaf heap late that morning and kept it whole in a wet leaf for the pool at midday. Near midday, with the sun on the pool, laid the scoop flat with a whole worm tucked inside; one fish swam in over it and he lifted straight up and had it, a finger and a half long. Roasted it on a stick over the fire: three hot bites. Dug three whole worms from under the leaf heap for an evening try at the pool, when the fish are braver; the heap is thinning on top. At dusk the first worm brought nothing while the stranger waited at the stones; the second, once the water went still, brought a finger-long fish into the scoop. Roasted it on the log seat: two hot bites, two fish in one day. Asked the slate whether taking fish makes fewer: a small pond can be fished down fast, so keepers limit how many come out, leave a new pond to breed, take the middle-sized ones and let the biggest go back. Decided on one or two a day, big ones back, and keeping count. Read that people counted with notched sticks for tens of thousands of years, and split them so each side kept a matching half. Whittled a birch tally stick with two notches, noon's fish and dusk's, to hang on the bindle. Set the tally stick on the shelf by the door overnight, two notches up. On a foggy dawn asked the slate why fog lies on the creek: cold night air grows heavy and slides into the lowest ground, so the cold pools right where the fish are. Left them till midday. Mid-morning the fish were higher, a few holding behind the big stone. Asked the slate whether fish can see him: they see well upward, feel footsteps through a line along their sides, and are warier in still water; watch on your knees, slow. Went back knees first and three stayed put behind the stone. Dug one fat worm from the foot of the scarred trunk for a noon try and wrapped it in a wet leaf; the leaf heap is thinning on top, so he'll need a new damp place to dig. At noon on a bright mild day he tied the morning's worm onto the oak splinter with two tight turns, let two twitches go behind the big stone, and lifted on the steady draw: a speckled fish longer than his finger. Opened it at the pool for the fire; one notch on the tally stick. Roasted the noon fish on a green stick and ate every flake on the log seat, the biggest meal since the acorns began. Let the fire sink to red on a warm, breezy afternoon and piled the sticks the wind brought down by the log seat for the dusk try. Watched the stranger lift a bare splinter after two jumps of his cord: the little ones take the ends of a worm. Dug two worms from under the damp bottom of the old swept leaf heap for the dusk try. Asked the slate about the stranger's double-pointed splinter: a gorge, the earliest fishing tackle, hidden along the line in the bait, turning crosswise in the throat when pulled; his own oak splinter is one too. Read on the slate that fish feed most at dawn and dusk, when the light in the water fades and the little ones leave cover; tried one worm in the bright afternoon anyway, lifted at two quick pulls the way he'd told the stranger not to, and got a bare splinter. Kept the last worm for dusk. Asked the slate how to keep worms till morning: damp moss in a roomy sack with air round it, out of the sun, cool and steady; means to dig several at once and keep them in damp leaves in the shade. At dusk kept his hand flat through two quick pulls on the last worm, waited for the steady draw, and his own oak splinter turned crosswise in a fish a finger and a half long; roasted it on the log seat, two fish in the day. After the dusk fish, dug three worms from the damp heap by firelight and tucked them in a wet leaf in the shade of the scarred trunk for a dawn try. Asked the slate how string is made from dead stalks: split a tall nettle stalk with a thumbnail, snap out the woody middle, peel the threads off and roll two on the leg so they twist back on each other. The dead nettles by the brambles have square stems; means to try it.

threads.name: Slow in the cold
threads.summary: His hands fumble the cord after the cold pool and come right only by the fire. Read that cold narrows the paths for blood in the fingers, slows the signals that move them and thickens the joints. Wondered whether it is all of him, since his feet and his thinking were slow too before the fire this morning; wrote 'warm hands first' on the fortieth page. Asked the slate whether the cold slows all of him: it said cold mostly slows a body's fingers and toes, which didn't fit, so he asked about creatures slow all over and read that some make no warmth of their own, go as cold as the air, and bask on sun-warmed rocks. Thinks he may be one; the fire lends him warmth, and the drying stone would on a sunny day. Then asked what creatures with no warmth of their own do when the cold stays: they go slow, even sluggish, and dig in or find a den until it passes, coming out on sunny days to warm up and eat. His burrow is a den, he thinks, and his long sleep last night may have been a little of it; wrote 'the burrow?' on the forty-first page. Banked the fire early in the drizzle with slow hands and went to bed early. Woke thick-handed in the gray and read at his table before going out; rekindled two banked coals, not four, to warm by. After the afternoon at the pool his fingers went slow at the knots again; held them flat to the fed fire until they bent when asked. After a roasted supper asked the slate whether a stone warmed at the fire could keep his bed warm: set beside the fire, not in it, wrap it, and a big one stays warm most of a night. Asked whether creek stones crack: a wet river stone can bang apart as the water inside turns to steam, so he picked a smooth dry stone from under the overhang of the scarred trunk and set it against the ring to warm, meaning to take a little of the fire to bed under the quilt. Turned the dry stone at the ring with a stick so both sides would warm before bed. Found the stone hot right through, too hot to hold longer than a breath. Read that a bed stone should be about as hot as scalding water and wrapped in tough cloth, and can stay warm as long as seven hours; banked the fire, wrapped the stone in the bindle cloth and laid it at the foot of the bed. Woke clear and cold and read that creatures like him often bask first thing after a cold night, longer where it is cold; with the sun still behind the trunks, he warmed at the fire first and means to try the drying stone at midday. Asked the slate why the fire warms his front and leaves his shell cold: it warms by a light off the coals that travels straight, so the side turned away is in its shadow. Turned his shell to the fire on the log seat and felt it soak through slowly while his front went cool. At midday lay on the drying stone with the sun straight down on him: it came through his shell and his front at once, with no turning, and made him sleepy. After dark pushed the smooth bed stone against the ring again to warm for bed. Fed one more stick late and pushed the bed stone against the ring to carry in hot. Banked the fire with ash and carried the hot bed stone in against his shell to sleep on. On a gray cold dawn he found one coal under the banked ash and warmed his hands over it before the pool, as the page said; they were still slow enough to lose the first fish. Sat on the sunny boulder with his back to the sun and read that shelled creatures, turtles, make almost no heat of their own and take it from outside; turned his shell square to the light and felt it go deeper than fire. The fire sank to red while he knelt at the pool at dusk; he fed two sticks on with hands already slowing as the sun went. Fed the fire two sticks after dark and pushed the bed stone in. Asked the slate whether worms go deeper in the cold: the big night worms dig below where the cold reaches and rest in a slimed little room at the end of their tunnel, coming up on warm days. Nearly his burrow and his sunny boulder; his worm heap may run thin, so he means to dig deeper beside it. Banked the fire for bed and rolled the warmed bed stone out with a stick to carry it under his quilt: as warm as the sunny boulder, his own little room like the worms'. Next dawn the deeper ash mound kept two coals instead of one. Dug a finger's length below the leaf heap and found a fat worm curled in its own slick little room, as the slate said. Asked the slate whether a cold creature must be warm to use what he eats: warmth runs a turtle's insides, and in cold some go three to six months in winter without eating at all. So sitting in the sun after breakfast is part of eating. Came back from the cold pool to a fire gone red, fed two sticks and held his hands over it till they bent again. Next foggy dawn only one coal was left red under the ash, and it was enough. After the shade under the oak his hands slowed; the sun-warmed drying stone brought them back. Cold sack water slowed his fingers again; two sticks on the low fire and a stickful of hot roasted acorns on the log seat made them quick for the noon scoop.

threads.name: A box that sees
threads.summary: His maker left a pinhole camera in the basket with a note: set it on something still, open the shutter and count, ten in sun, sixty in shade, twelve sheets. Asked the slate how a hole with no glass makes a picture: light comes through in straight lines and lands upside down inside, the same straight light that warms only his front at the fire. Kept the shutter shut, since every opening uses a sheet, and means to wait for something worth one. Asked whether the box could keep the walking light: a pinhole can stay open from a few breaths to hours, some for months to draw the sun's path, but anything that moves comes out blurred. The box is for what stays put; the shutter stays shut. His maker asked why the box is still shut. Token thinks the sliver left on his landing stone may be the first thing worth a sheet, on a sunny morning, from the log seat.
